track: Track A adjacent official professional correction
journal_volume_issue_year: New York Board of Regents enforcement actions, June and July 1997
article_title: Enforcement-action summaries for Helen M. Fogarty (a/k/a Helen Moses) and Marc Rice
author: New York State Education Department Office of the Professions; New York State Board of Regents
community_group: Sullivan Institute / Sullivanians, linked by lead finding F-156
page_locator: June 12, 1997 Psychology entry; July 18, 1997 Psychology entry
source_access: official regulator summaries and explanation of New York professional-discipline authority inspected
evidence_type: two final psychology-license dispositions with conduct-specific public summaries
exact_factual_observation: On June 12, 1997 the Board revoked Helen M. Fogarty's psychology license and imposed a $15,000 fine after findings summarized as verbal abuse of a patient, multiple relationships, signing billing statements for services not provided, attempted undue influence on a patient to drop misconduct accusations, and sexual relations with two supervisees. On July 18, 1997 it revoked Marc Rice's psychology license after findings summarized as verbal abuse, directing a patient to drink alcohol, directing the patient not to be alone with her children and to cease communication with her parents, multiple relationships, and direction to have multiple sexual relationships.
what_source_establishes: An external professional regulator can investigate and terminate licensed authority for conduct that crosses therapy, supervision, billing, influence over complaints, sexuality, and family contact. The official record independently corroborates later professional discipline for two people named in the review-level Sullivanian lead.
what_source_does_not_establish: The summaries do not name the Sullivan Institute, reproduce the complete charges or evidence, adjudicate the Pappo custody matter, establish misconduct by every Sullivanian therapist, prove that publicity caused discipline, or report patient, child, family, institutional, or later safeguarding outcomes. Revocation is not proof of recovery or complete correction.
author_interpretation: The Office of the Professions states that it investigates and prosecutes covered professional misconduct and that the Board of Regents makes the final disposition; the entries report findings of guilt and revocation.
alternative_interpretation: The public summaries may omit defenses, evidentiary detail, charge-level variation, chronology, and any appeal. The Sullivanian link depends on the separately limited F-156 source lead, not on organizational naming in the official pages.
response_process: conduct complaint or charge; professional investigation and prosecution; Board of Regents disposition; license revocation and, for Fogarty/Moses, a fine. No internal community process, child advocate, custody review, restitution, or follow-up appears in the record.
outcome: Two psychology licenses were revoked. The record supplies no later child safety, family-contact, patient-recovery, compensation, institution-wide reform, or compliance outcome.
transferability: High for separating therapy and supervision from family, complaint, billing, and intimate authority and for preserving a regulator route outside the therapist's institution. Low for inferring group-wide conduct or completed safeguarding, and zero for transferring licensing or custody power to a private community.
likely_article_destination: Community as therapist / founderism / children / external legal couplings / outcome dashboard
notes: Use the disposition dates, license and calendar numbers, and summarized findings only as official regulatory facts. Retrieve full charges, findings, hearing files, surrender records for other named therapists, and appellate material before reconstructing the entire professional sequence. Do not treat a license endpoint as a child outcome.

track: Track A adjacent official inquiry and ongoing safeguarding
article_title: Gloriavale findings, correction history, and Recommendation 88
author: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions
page_locator: Part 7 chapter 5 paras 333 and 409; Part 7 chapter 8 paras 715-716; Part 9 chapter 5 paras 528-531; Recommendation 88
source_access: official final-report HTML, inquiry findings, institutional-response material, OIA briefing summaries, and recommendation text inspected
evidence_type: independent royal-commission finding and correction record with historical and later government-response evidence
exact_factual_observation: The Inquiry found that a Gloriavale policy in force from 1989 to 2002 prevented reporting crimes to secular agencies and limited outside contact; it also found that leadership routinely failed to respond adequately and that reports had been handled by the founder until the mid-1990s, before his later conviction for sexual offences including against young people. The report recorded a government coordination function operating from August 2022 to December 2023 and December 2023 briefings describing continuing child-wellbeing risks and agency responses. Recommendation 88 calls for all practicable government steps to ensure ongoing safety at Gloriavale.
what_source_establishes: A written or understood internal bar on secular reporting is itself a safeguarding failure when the same authority chain handles allegations. Official correction must preserve direct external intake, evidence, cross-agency coordination, independent oversight, survivor participation, and continuing outcome review rather than treating one prosecution, safety plan, or inquiry as institutional closure.
what_source_does_not_establish: The Inquiry does not establish exact prevalence, adjudicate every reported event, prove the current status of proceedings cited in December 2023 briefings, show that Recommendation 88 has been implemented, or supply a complete later-outcome panel for children, survivors, families, alleged perpetrators, or the institution. It does not authorize private investigation, punishment, removal, or custody action.
author_interpretation: The Commission attributed much Gloriavale abuse to authoritarian control combined with spiritual authority and concluded that ongoing safety required government action, independent monitoring, and faith-sector care standards.
alternative_interpretation: Multiple agencies and internal actors may have taken measures not captured by the selected sections, and criminal or civil proceedings address narrower questions than system safety. Even justified external intervention can fail without continuity, resources, family contact, survivor support, and implementation measures.
response_process: disclosure or observed harm; internally blocked or inadequate response; later survivor evidence, police and official records; royal-commission investigation and institutional hearing; cross-agency coordination and safety-plan activity; published findings and Recommendation 88; future implementation and outcome review still required.
outcome: The final report created a public correction record and specific ongoing-safety recommendation. It also recorded that the temporary coordination function had ended while official briefings still identified risks. The source does not demonstrate completed correction or later safety.
transferability: High for independent intake, preservation of screening reasons and policy records, survivor participation, cross-agency coordination, oversight, and explicit implementation follow-up. Low for direct transfer of state powers; residents may report and preserve observable evidence but may not adjudicate, coerce, or assume child-protection authority.
likely_article_destination: Protected reporting / children / founderism / external legal couplings / outcome dashboard
notes: Historical source window and later-context dates must remain explicit. The report's description of pending charges and safety arrangements is a dated record, not a 2026 status statement. Keep children here as alleged victims; do not merge this finding with the dangerous-child actor branch.

track: Track A adjacent statutory inquiry and external reporting
article_title: Child protection in religious organisations and settings investigation report
author: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse Inquiry Panel
community_group: Jesus Fellowship Church / New Creation Christian Community
page_locator: Part B para 13; Part C paras 48 and 61-62; Part H conclusions and recommendations
source_access: complete official web report, Jesus Fellowship evidence section, conclusions, recommendations, cited public-hearing transcript, and police-document references inspected
evidence_type: statutory inquiry synthesis combining survivor testimony, police evidence, prosecution outcomes, sector analysis, and recommendations
exact_factual_observation: The Inquiry recorded testimony that children who disclosed within the Jesus Fellowship could be disbelieved or blamed while an accused person might be prayed over or moved, and that reputation, distrust of outsiders, and a cycle of forgiveness obstructed external reporting. In 2013 the Church invited disclosures; those disclosures went to Northamptonshire Police and Operation Lifeboat. The report states that seven suspects were tried and six were convicted of offences relating to 11 children. Its conclusions state that internal discipline cannot substitute for external reporting, justice, redress, or risk assessment.
what_source_establishes: Disclosure intake must be child-accessible and independent of reputation, forgiveness, reconciliation, and membership discipline. Allegations, internal findings, police evidence, convictions, survivor support, professional risk assessment, redress, and later safety are distinct records. Passing disclosures to police can produce accountability, but it does not by itself measure institutional repair or survivor recovery.
what_source_does_not_establish: The thematic report does not adjudicate every allegation, provide a full prevalence denominator, identify every accused person, report later child or survivor wellbeing, complete the then-ongoing investigation, or establish post-report implementation by the closed Fellowship or successor bodies. Its sector recommendations are not evidence that every organization complied.
author_interpretation: The Inquiry concluded that religious child-protection practice was uneven, under-reporting likely significant, internal discipline an inadequate sole response, victim-focused policies and whistleblowing necessary, and external oversight broadly supported.
alternative_interpretation: The insurer-requested disclosure exercise, police investigation, convictions, later closure, and any subsequent redress arose through several institutions and incentives; the report does not isolate which step caused disclosure or safety. Criminal convictions concern proven offences, not all institutional allegations or system-wide repair.
response_process: survivor or witness disclosure; 2013 public invitation; transfer of forms to police; Operation Lifeboat investigation; arrests and interviews; seven trials and six convictions; further investigation; statutory inquiry review; recommendations for victim-focused policy, professional advice, training, education oversight, and external reporting.
outcome: Six perpetrators were convicted of offences relating to 11 children according to the inquiry record. The source reports no complete survivor-recovery, redress, successor-organization, or later safeguarding outcome, so conviction and organizational closure cannot be counted as full correction.
transferability: High for separating pastoral care and forgiveness from evidence testing, police referral, independent adjudication, survivor services, risk management, and outcome review. Medium for sector design. Zero for community-run criminal investigation, coercion, diagnosis, custody, or punishment.
likely_article_destination: Protected reporting / children / fair process / founderism / external legal couplings / outcome dashboard
notes: Published September 2, 2021. Preserve the distinction among witness evidence, allegations received by police, people tried, and people convicted. The inquiry's quoted labels and witness characterizations are not diagnoses or admission-screen inputs.
